paper_title: VideoNexus: Video Perception Beyond the Reasoning Context

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Understanding long videos requires locating evidence, resolving visual details, and integrating observations into an answer. Even when relevant evidence is present, performing these operations within long, dense visual sequences burdens both perception and reasoning. Video agents enable selective inspection, but returning frames to the planner still accumulates visual information in its reasoning context. Delegating perception reduces this burden, yet sparse sampling can miss decisive details, and per-frame descriptions can preserve context growth. We introduce VideoNexus, a training-free framework that separates detailed video perception from evidence-driven planning and reasoning. The planner controls where to inspect, what to resolve, and how densely to sample. Perception sub-agents process native audio-video in independent contexts and return compact, temporally grounded evidence for iterative search and verification. Using Gemini 3.8 Flash for both planning and perception, VideoNexus achieves 88.6% accuracy on full LVBench, exceeding same-backbone static ingestion and built-in agentic processing by 3.6 and 1.1 points, respectively, at 44% of the latter's measured API cost. A paired LVBench subset ablation shows lower planner input and higher accuracy. With Kimi K3 as the shared backbone, VideoNexus improves over the official Video-GAIA ReAct harness by 8.5 points in our evaluation. These results support compact evidence exchange for combining detailed observation with efficient planning and reasoning.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Understanding long video involves finding the evidence that matters to question, examining its visual details, and reasoning about how observations fit together. These operations are closely related: an initial observation may suggest location to revisit, detail to verify, or new question to resolve. Even when all relevant evidence is included in the input, model must locate and interpret it among substantial amounts of unrelated visual information. one-hour video sampled at one frame per second produces hundreds of thousands of visual tokens [36]. Static ingestion places evidence localization, perception and reasoning within this shared multimodal context [2, 13]; denser input provides more detail but also increases the information the model must process together. Video agents allow this process to unfold through interaction: the model chooses where to look, evaluates the returned evidence, and decides whether another observation is needed [9, 37, 38, 56]. EVA [58] learns querydriven observation policies, and VideoTemp-o3 [22] jointly learns temporal grounding and question answering with localization refinement. Alongside these advances in selecting observations, the interface that delivers them to the reasoning context remains consequential. When tools return raw frames or clips directly to the planner, visual inputs accumulate in the context that also guides subsequent actions and integrates evidence (figure 1a). Adaptive selection changes which media is read, but the planner continues to process that media alongside its reasoning history. In our controlled comparison, this coupled design uses 1.47 as much planner input as returning evidence from independent perception calls (section 4.4). Delegating perception to separate models addresses this context burden and is already established in video agents. VideoSeek [17] and VideoXAgent [45], for example, allow planner to act on textual observations. First, sparse sampling can omit brief events or fine details needed to verify an answer, motivating inspection at density appropriate to the local task. Second, text interface can preserve the dependence between observation size and sampling density. VideoSeeks global scan returns one description per frame, averaging 28 returned tokens per frame read in our re-run (section 4.5). Increasing its scan budget would therefore also lengthen the report retained for reasoning. Separating model calls alone does not determine either how closely the agent can inspect moment or how much information it must carry forward. We study how to give video agents access to detailed observations while controlling what each observation adds to the reasoning context. The required detail varies across the process: broad exploration locates candidate moments, while local verification may require denser sampling around specific event. This motivates treating each perception call as focused evidence-gathering task, with its location and sampling density chosen by the planner and its output organized around the question being resolved. We introduce VideoNexus, training-free framework for video perception beyond the reasoning context (figure 1b). The Planner formulates local tasks, selects intervals and sampling rates, integrates returned evidence, and decides when to stop. Perception sub-agents examine native audiovideo in independent, short-lived contexts. Overview returns compact set of candidate intervals for navigation; Inspect returns Finding with claims anchored to the absolute source timeline and explicit evidence or uncertainty status. Both global and local reports limit the information returned instead of describing every sampled frame. In the final configuration, small local evidence cards accompany visual findings for verification. The planner can thus request further detail without retaining the complete perceptual input from each call. VideoNexus runs on stock agent runtime with Model Context Protocol tools and requires no training. Our experiments examine context use, observation size and task performance. With Gemini 3.8 Flash as the shared backbone, paired LVBench ablation reduces planner input by 32% while increasing accuracy from 86.5% to 89.0% in that run. On full LVBench [36], VideoNexus achieves 88.6%, compared with 85.0% for static ingestion and 87.5% for Geminis agentic mode, at 44% of the latters measured API cost. It reads 621 frames per question on average and outperforms same-backbone VideoSeek re-run by 7.2 points at lower cost; the comparison also differs in audio access, analyzed in the supplementary material. With Kimi K3 as the shared backbone on VideoGAIA [53], it improves over the official ReAct harness by 8.5 points in our evaluation; further experiments examine transfer across planner models. Our contributions are: We analyze the coupling between video observation and reasoning context, including how per-frame text can preserve this dependence after perception is delegated. We introduce VideoNexus, combining planner-directed perception with bounded, temporally grounded evidence exchange for global exploration and local verification. We evaluate the design through controlled ablations and per-call measurements, together with same-backbone accuracycost comparisons and transfer experiments. 2 VideoNexus: Video Perception Beyond the Reasoning Context

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Long contexts and video representations. Frontier MLLMs accept long native videos [2, 7, 13, 15]; other work extends context [55] or compresses visual tokens [32]. Long-video benchmarks expose difficulties in retrieving and reasoning over detailed evidence [11, 36, 41], and required sampling density varies across questions [29]. Textonly studies likewise show that access to long context does not ensure effective use of its contents [19]. Real-time systems support full-duplex audiovisual interaction [8] or parallel listening, writing and speaking [54], addressing interaction constraints distinct from long-video evidence search. Language-mediated representations [50, 51] and searchable video memories [3, 9, 25, 37, 56] organize evidence for later reasoning. Several methods combine initial representations with query-conditioned retrieval, refinement or inspection [23, 26, 38, 49]; they are not uniformly fixed, question-independent indices. Sequential memory construction [4, 5] and compositional visual programs [14, 27, 33] offer further ways to structure perception. Precomputed representations can amortize work across questions, while query-time inspection can revisit details omitted from the initial representation. We focus on the interface between such inspection and the planners reasoning context. Learned policies and working memory. OmniAgent [42] learns active perception; EVA [58] trains summary planactionreflection loop; and VideoTemp-o3 [22] jointly trains temporal grounding and question answering with localization refinement. VideoSEAL [28] separates planning from final answer authority for visual verification, whereas VideoLoop [43] provides plug-and-play working-memory rewriting. These address different parts of an agents evidence-processing pipeline. In adjacent settings, Thyme [57] learns image-processing code for visual reasoning, SpatialReward [24] uses explicit spatial reasoning to evaluate image edits, and DeltaVid [46] improves fine-grained video perception through cross-video difference supervision. VideoNexus studies training-free observation interface. Learned policies, improved perception and compact evidence exchange are complementary; our experiments do not compare against these trained policies. Query-time and delegated perception. Recent agents combine query-conditioned observation with tool orchestration. AVP [39] separates coarse scanning from detailed inspection; VideoResearcher [48] evolves tools through solving and tool-refinement loops; VideoXAgent [45] integrates broad tool set; and VideoSeek [17] navigates through overview, skim and focus operations. Related approaches explore multi-agent coordination, observation routing and task-specific tools [10, 12, 16, 34, 35, 44, 52]; GoP-Agent [6] exploits compressed-video motion information. These systems differ in their memory and observation interfaces. Delegated perception is established practice. Our focus is how returned reports scale with media inspected during global navigation and local verification. In our VideoSeek re-run, global scanning returns per-frame descriptions, while local focus already returns concise answer. VideoNexus returns up to eight candidate intervals from Overview and task-specific Findings from Inspect; section 4.5 measures their output growth. LAVE [40] instead injects latent visual evidence into reasoning. Our main configuration also retains limited visual evidence through small cards, while explicit uncertainty can prompt further inspection. Commercial modes and evaluation. OpenAIs o3 reasons with images, and Gemini provides agentic video processing. The Qwen3.8-Omni report [30] also evaluates agentic video understanding. Open-world agents combine video reasoning with research [21]; VideoDR [18] and Video-GAIA [53] provide benchmarks with ReActstyle baselines [47]. Static ingestion remains competitive [31], motivating our same-backbone static comparison. TRACE [20] evaluates visual evidence coverage. REPAIR [1] highlights variation across repeated agent executions: our full-set paired tests address within-run differences, not repeat-run reproducibility. Anthropics multi-agent research system also delegates research to sub-agents that return condensed results. VideoNexus examines this design for video, where the detail of each observation and the size of its report can be controlled separately.

sections.title: 3.2 VideoNexus
sections.content: VideoNexus consists of Planner that never receives the video stream and set of perception sub-agents exposed as tools (figure 2; schematic and the full tool list are in the supplementary material). The Planner receives the question and short policy (a skill of about ten sentences) that imposes no fixed call order and states that transcripts may contain errors, that Overview returns navigation clues rather than evidence, that visual claims require visual evidence, and to stop once the answer is supported. Every perception call runs an independent model call on native media, in context that is discarded afterwards. Transcribe runs ASR once per video, independently of the question, and returns segments with absolute times; it is cached and shared across questions. Overview performs query-conditioned, globally sparse scan of the native video (at most 1 fps and 1,024 frames, at low resolution, with the full audio track) and returns short summary and up to eight candidate intervals, each with an observation, relevance estimate and an uncertainty note. Its prompt states that sparse sampling cannot establish absence and forbids choosing an answer option, so Overview is locator, not judge; it is limited to two calls per question. Inspect, the main evidence source, reads an interval [𝑠, 𝑒] at frame rate chosen by the Planner, with an open-ended local task such as describe what the person places on the red armchair and when. The skill asks the Planner to phrase local tasks neutrally, and the perception prompt forbids selecting an option of the parent question, so Finding reports what the interval shows rather than echoing 4 VideoNexus: Video Perception Beyond the Reasoning Context the Planners hypothesis. For open-world questions the same pattern extends to source-resolution crops and to web search and page extraction [53]; the LVBench runs use only Transcribe, Overview and Inspect (with crops).

sections.title: 3.3 The Finding protocol
sections.content: Each Inspect call returns JSON Finding with status {ok, absent, uncertain, failed}, where absent refers only to the sampled observation; one-sentence conclusion; what was observed; and evidence items {claim, [𝑡0, 𝑡1], modality} with modality {visual, audio, audio_visual} and times on the absolute source timeline. The harness validates every Finding: evidence whose time range falls outside the inspected interval is dropped, and an ok status without remaining evidence is downgraded to uncertain. This validates structure and temporal range, not factual correctness. Overview caps candidates at eight; Inspect has no eight-item cap. Both have generation budget independent of frame count. Bounded evidence exchange refers to this budget and compact report design; section 4.5 measures actual output growth. The final configuration returns each visual Finding with an evidence card: single contact sheet containing at most six source frames selected from its cited evidence intervals, each labeled with its absolute time. Dense video and audio remain in the perception context. The card grows with evidence, not with inspected duration; on full LVBench it amounts to 3.3 images and 2% of the Planners input tokens per question, with model-dependent effects on accuracy (section 4.4).

sections.title: 3.4 Native timeline addressing and implementation
sections.content: Perception calls reference the original video file with start and end offsets and frame rate, instead of cutting and re-encoding clips, and the perception model then reports times on the original timeline: in probe with neutral prompts, all 12 responses returned absolute source times, while physically cropped clip returned times relative to its own start (the supplementary material). Findings from different calls, the transcript and the Overview can therefore be compared directly. Each question runs in an isolated headless Claude Code session whose only built-in tool is the skill loader; perception tools are served over the Model Context Protocol, and local bridge routes the Planner to any provider, replaying Geminis thought signatures across turns. Unless stated otherwise, the Planner and sub-agents share the model and high thinking effort, with at most 32 turns, 256 frames per Inspect and 10 local calls. Cumulative-budget implementation and observed usage are detailed in the supplementary material. The harness requires no training and no access to model weights.

sections.title: 4.1 Setup
sections.content: Benchmarks. LVBench [36] contains 1,549 four-way multiple-choice questions on 103 hour-scale videos in six categories: entity recognition (ER, 560), event understanding (EU, 526), key information retrieval (KIR, 196), reasoning (Rea, 147), summarization (Sum, 55) and temporal grounding (TG, 65). We report accuracy on the full set and count invalid outputs as wrong. Ablations use fixed 200-question development subset stratified by category and covering all 103 videos (dev-200); they are paired comparisons inside that subset, while the main Gemini 3.8 system comparison uses the full set, including these development questions. Video-GAIA [53] contains 271 openended questions (L1: 62, L2: 209) whose answers require video evidence and web search; both arms are scored by one binary semantic judge (Kimi K3) with the same prompt and reference answers (the supplementary material). Models and baselines. The main experiments use Gemini 3.8 Flash for both the Planner and perception, with high thinking effort and low media resolution; cross-model experiments use Gemini 3.0 Flash and Kimi K3. Hosted models are accessed through APIs; the reported backbone is shared across the main comparison. Static feeds the whole native video with audio in one call at 1 fps, capped at 2,048 frames. Gemini Agentic is Googles server-side agentic media-processing mode with high thinking; it reports the media it navigates as image tokens, from which we estimate 464 frames per question (the supplementary material). VideoSeek [17] is re-run from its official code on the same Gemini 3.8 Flash back-end at its published perception budget, with its own prompts, tools and budgets; we drive it through the providers native interface with thought signatures replayed, without which over half of its steps return empty (the supplementary material). VideoSeek has no audio path, and LVBench ships no subtitles, so it never receives speech; we quantify this asymmetry in the supplementary material. On Video-GAIA we run the oﬀicial ReAct agent, which keeps 20 uniformly sampled frames in context. 5 VideoNexus: Video Perception Beyond the Reasoning Context Cost. We report API cost per question at list prices ($0.75 per million fresh input tokens, $0.075 per million cached input tokens, $3.75 per million output tokens including thinking), and cold-start every question: caches shared across questions are repriced as fresh input, while caching within question is kept (the supplementary material). ASR cost is excluded for all methods.

Against Static this is +3.6 points (90 questions won, 34 lost, exact McNemar 𝑝=5107). Against Gemini Agentic it is +1.1 points at 44% of the cost; that difference, 57 won against 40 lost, is not significant (𝑝=0.10). Their context organization and reasoning usage differ, but the closed baseline prevents isolating the source of this cost gap (the supplementary material). Against the VideoSeek re-run, which also delegates perception, VideoNexus is correct on 153 questions VideoSeek misses and wrong on 42 it answers (88.6% against 81.4%, 𝑝=51016). The two use similar fresh input token counts per question, 118.2k for VideoSeek and 118.7k for VideoNexus (figure 3b), while processing 123 still-image frames and 621 native-video frames with audio, respectively. They differ in generated output: VideoSeek emits 26.2k tokens per question against our 12.4k, and output is billed at five times the fresh-input price, accounting for most of the cost difference. VideoNexus also needs fewer model calls, 9.7 per question (6.1 planner turns, 3.6 perception calls) against 18.6. It leads in five of six categories, by 2.7 points on reasoning and 3.6 on summarization; temporal grounding is the exception (92.3 against 90.8 for Gemini Agentic, one question). Much of the remaining headroom is shared: 122 of VideoNexuss 177 errors are also errors of both Static and Gemini Agentic.

In the coupled arms, get_frames appends the native low-resolution audiovideo interval to the Planners context; in the decoupled arm, inspect_frames returns Finding from an independent call to the same model. Decoupling reduces Planner input from 18.1M to 12.3M tokens (32%), while accuracy rises from 86.5% (173/200) to 89.0% (178/200) in this paired run. Total cost increases by 5%, with perception processed in separate calls. The 2.5-point accuracy increase comprises eight corrected answers and three regressions; this difference is not statistically significant (exact McNemar 𝑝=0.23). Removing Transcribe from the coupled agent doubles Overview calls (92 187) and raises cost by 45%: speech is cheap localization cue. Panel (a) disables evidence cards to isolate delegated local perception. Panel (b) asks whether selected visual evidence adds value to text reports: local cards raise Gemini 3.0 Flash from 74.5% to 79.5% and Gemini 3.8 Flash from 89.0% (178/200) to 90.0% (180/200). Both show gains, with larger observed increase for Gemini 3.0; differing harness configurations prevent attributing that difference solely to backbone capability. Adding global Overview frames on top of local cards reduces Gemini 3.0 accuracy to 75.5%. These results motivate retaining compact local visual memory alongside text, while delegating dense perception. VideoNexus: Video Perception Beyond the Reasoning Context

sections.content: Figure 4. Report size versus observed frames on full LVBench (loglog axes). Coral dots are 4,376 Inspect calls with decile means; distributions summarize tools with nearly fixed frame counts. Dashed lines mark 1, 10, and 100 returned tokens per frame. Global scanning and local answering produce different report sizes, as discussed in the text. We measure how strongly the size of returned observation grows with the media inspected. Figure 4 measures it on every perception call of the full run (per-tool table in the supplementary material). Overview consumes 141k media tokens on average, 1,019 frames plus the complete audio track, and returns 740 tokens, 191 reduction, with loglog slope of 0.00 against perceived tokens (𝑟=0.01), indicating little association within the observed range. inspect_frames, which is asked for detail, grows sub-linearly with slope 0.18: between its lowest and highest decile of perceived media, frames rise 16.8 while returned text rises 1.67 (308 514 tokens). Overview limits its candidate list, and Inspect answers local task in structured report. These measurements support weak output growth; they do not establish constant output size or calibrated confidence. VideoSeeks scanning tools return approximately one description per frame: 63.8 descriptions per 64-frame overview and 14.4 per 16-frame skim, or 28 and 63 returned tokens per frame read. Its query-answering focus returns 4.4 tokens per frame and is also concise. This baseline already uses concise local answers; the measured distinction is in the reports used for global navigation. In the full run, perception reads 621 frames per question on average, while the Planners context at its final turn holds 19.6k tokens on average, system prompt and skill included.

sections.title: 4.8 Failure modes
sections.content: On the 153 questions VideoSeek misses and VideoNexus answers, VideoSeek takes 8.5 steps against its 6.2 average and scans globally first on 76%. Continued interaction does not always resolve missing evidence; sampling and action-selection effects remain intertwined. On the 42 that go the other way our trajectories run long, 9.7 turns against typical 6.1, with Overview used on 29 of them and skipped on 13. Local inspection can therefore remain unsuccessful even after global scan. On Video-GAIA, 26 of 28 inspected cases find the right interval, while crops are readable enough to identify the target in 16 of 27 cases. This small qualitative sample points to spatial readability as remaining difficulty.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: Long-video agents must decide both what to observe and what to retain for reasoning. VideoNexus supports this process through planner-directed perception in independent contexts and compact, temporally grounded reports for global navigation and local verification. The paired ablation reduces planner input while increasing accuracy in that run, and per-call measurements show slowly growing reports across full LVBench. With Gemini 3.8 Flash, it reaches 88.6% on LVBench at 44% of the built-in agentic modes measured API cost. With Kimi K3, it improves over the official Video-GAIA harness by 8.5 points in our evaluation. These results support focused evidence exchange for video agents, subject to imperfect perception and the development and comparison limits discussed in the supplementary material. The visual-memory ablations motivate retaining selected evidence for verification alongside text reports. Future work should examine how observation density and retained evidence adapt to uncertainty across tasks and model capabilities. 9 VideoNexus: Video Perception Beyond the Reasoning Context

On full LVBench Finding averages 401 tokens for 5.0k media tokens (62 frames plus audio), and between the lowest and highest decile of media perceived (12 and 198 frames) its text grows only 1.67. Output and sampling limits. Overview truncates candidates to eight intervals; Inspect has no eight-item cap on its evidence array. Both use maximum generation budget of 32,768 tokens, including thinking, and prompts encourage compact output. The frozen runners configure 256 frames per local call, ten calls and 2,048 cumulative frames. The direct-media implementation enforces all three; the delegated path bypasses the cumulative check. However, the largest recorded cumulative count is 1,024 across the available delegated development traces and 1,624 across the 1,549 saved full-run trajectories. Thus recorded delegated observations remain below the configured limit, despite the enforcement difference. 14 VideoNexus: Video Perception Beyond the Reasoning Context Earlier model configuration. The Gemini 3.0 result uses an earlier harness without ASR, combines the development subset and the remaining questions, and compares with medium-resolution static baseline. It supports applicability beyond the main backbone but does not isolate model swap in an otherwise identical harness.

sections.title: B Baselines
sections.content: Gemini Agentic. The mode was run with high thinking; 37 of 1,549 questions that failed repeatedly at high thinking were retried at medium. It reports the media it navigated as IMAGE tokens under toolUsePromptTokenCount, never as video or audio, and for 92% of the questions that count is an exact multiple of 66, the per-frame cost of low-resolution video, so the navigated frames enter the planning models own context as images (appendix L). Dividing by 66 estimates 464 frames per question on average (median 150, maximum 12,106), which describes its observation volume without isolating the cause of its cost. Reproducing VideoSeek. The baseline runs VideoSeeks released code with its own prompts, tools, step budget and sampling configuration (frame_sampling_factor 4, overview_base 16, skim_base 4, focus_base 4, max_steps 20, max_tokens 32768, temperature 1.0, seed 42): 64-frame overview, 16-frame skims, and 16second focus windows at 1 fps in the tool description. We substitute the backbone and adapt the provider interface as detailed below. Its agent asks the model for plain-text thought and then makes second, tool-enabled call to parse that text into actions, so the function calls in its history are synthesized locally rather than returned by the provider. That design also asks for plan in prose with no tools attached, and on this back-end an unconstrained turn answers such prompt with call to one of the providers own built-in video tools instead, which reaches an OpenAI-style client as empty content: over half of the agents steps then come back with an empty thought (57.6% of its thoughts were lost when run that way), and its planner falls back to re-issuing the same overview until the step budget runs out. Gemini 3 also attaches an opaque thought signature to each model turn, and replaying function call without it is rejected. We therefore drive the baseline through the native streamGenerateContent interface, declare function calling off on exactly the turns VideoSeek means to be tool-free, replay each model turn with the signature it was issued, and flatten the locally synthesized call envelope, whose action text each observation already restates verbatim. We ran it at the high thinking level used by our own arms, above the medium its configuration requests, to align thinking effort; this is change from its default configuration. One asymmetry runs the other way and is discussed under Limitations: it reads no transcript and no audio. Two details of the released implementation matter for anyone repeating this. focus advertises 𝛼4 at 1 FPS to the planner but caps on frame indices rather than seconds, so any window longer than about half second yields the full 𝛼4 frames spread over it however long it is, which is why we take frames from the configured budget rather than from the tool description. And its subtitle window filter combines its two bounds with disjunction where conjunction is intended, making the filter no-op for any mid-video window.

sections.title: C Cost accounting
sections.content: Cold start. Static has cross-question cache hits because its video prefix repeats across questions on the same video; we reprice those hits as fresh input. The two agentic rows have none: over all 1,549 questions, the first model call of question is billed with zero cached tokens for both VideoNexus and the VideoSeek re-run, so every cache hit either one gets is hit on its own questions history and is kept. Pricing those within-question hits as fresh as well would read $0.184 for VideoNexus and $0.201 for VideoSeek, 1.09 ratio instead of 1.34; the ordering survives either basis. Sensitivity to media pricing. The provider bills the two transports differently: 66 tokens per frame for native video stream at low resolution, against per-image-part resolution tier for stills (264, 527, 1.1k and 2.2k prompt tokens per part, independent of the pixels in it) that VideoSeek leaves at its 1.1k-token default. The measured cost therefore reflects both harness behavior and provider-specific media pricing. Repricing every image part VideoSeek sent at each tier, and changing nothing else, gives $0.252 per question at the most expensive tier, $0.188 as it ran, $0.155 one tier down and $0.140 at the cheapest, against $0.140 for VideoNexus. At the cheapest tier the repriced costs are equal. Setting image charges to zero gives VideoSeek $0.125 per question, 89% of our cost; both calculations retain its measured accuracy. The repricing holds accuracy fixed without validating that assumption: 15 VideoNexus: Video Perception Beyond the Reasoning Context its overview packs eight frames into single montage image, so the cheapest tier would leave those eight frames 264 tokens between them, and its focus sends frames at full resolution in order to resolve detail. An arm measuring the accuracy cost of that tier is the one reprice we have not run. At the measured tier, the two harnesses use similar fresh input token counts, 118.2k fresh tokens per question against 118.7k, and differ 2.1 in output, which is priced at five times input; output is 52% of VideoSeeks bill and 33% of ours. All dollar figures are list prices of one model and should not be carried to another provider.

sections.title: H Qualitative analysis
sections.content: Of the 37 v0 errors on dev-200, 15 stem from localization or fine-grained identity, 8 from counting or ordering across segments, and 3 from mapping correct evidence to the wrong option. On the 153 questions VideoSeek misses and VideoNexus answers, VideoSeek took 8.5 steps against its own 6.2 average, called focus 630 times, and had scanned globally first on 76% of them: these traces show continued evidence seeking but do not identify sampling as the sole cause of failure. On the 42 that go the other way, our trajectories make 214 inspect_frames calls in total and use Overview on 29 questions. Detailed local inspection can remain unsuccessful even after global navigation. Figure 2 in the main paper follows one question (lvbench_10) through both kinds of call; appendix gives five further complete trajectories, including failure, and the behaviour of the loop over the full run. 18 VideoNexus: Video Perception Beyond the Reasoning Context

Table 8. Component ablations with VideoNexus v0 and Gemini 3.0 Flash on dev-200 (dev-100). Low Inspect resolution uses 72.9% fewer image tokens than high; the slim Skill prompt cuts Planner input by 46.8% for 1.5 points; the evidence-closure rule cuts turns by 26.5% and cost by 23.7%. Repeating one configuration twice moved it by 3 questions (79 and 82 of 100), which is the resolution of this table. Table 8 summarizes design choices made during development with an earlier version of the harness. Which visual information should reach the Planner was measured on the same subset and is reported in table 3. Forcing Overview to propose at least one candidate interval is better than letting it return none, and keeping the global timeline in addition to candidates is better than candidates alone. Separate atomic tools outperform single batched inspection tool by 5.5 points. Low-resolution Inspect is as accurate as high resolution while using 72.9% fewer image tokens. Giving Inspect the audio track and ASR improves accuracy by 2.5 points. We also tested several prompt-level policies that tell the Planner how to sample (density hints, joint multi-window inspection, mandatory cropping, explicit evidence-state receipts, neutral-task rules in the tool schema, dedicated counting tools). None provided convincing evidence of improvement on this development subset, and several reduced accuracy by 35 points; we report them as group because no individual policy separated from the baseline. These development results motivated minimal policy that leaves observation choices to the Planner, without establishing that this policy is generally optimal. Raising the turn limit from 10 to 14 was measured separately on 20 questions repeated three times and moved the mean from 10.00 to 10.67 correct while increasing tool calls by 32%, so the limit was left at the lower value. When does an agent help? Agentic perception is not free. On LongVideoBench with Gemini 3.0, the earlier harness loses 2.1 points on 15second clips and gains 13 points on videos longer than one minute. On the long split of Video-MME, where the static model already reaches 85.2%, it loses 4.0 points. Questions that depend on global temporal order (for example, ordering of scenes) are hurt by local inspection, whereas questions that require finding and identifying specific entity or event benefit most. These results suggest routing between static ingestion and the agent by video length and question type, which we leave to future work. This block was measured on an earlier version of the harness than the one in the main paper, so we report it for the direction of the effect rather than its magnitude. Inside Geminis agentic mode We analyzed traces of Geminis agentic media-processing mode on ten LVBench questions with Gemini 3.7 Flash, one of the documented models for this mode. The responses expose 46 thought signatures, of which only the ten final ones are decodable, and 28 thought summaries. On average the model performs 1.8 internal navigation steps per question. Tool-use token accounting reports image and text tokens but no audio tokens, and for 1,311 of the 1,429 full-LVBench questions where the mode navigated at all (92%) the image-token count is an exact multiple of 66, the per-frame cost of low-resolution video; the remaining counts exceed multiple of 66 by small amount, so some navigated images are not plain low-resolution frames. These observations suggest server-side media index that offers timestamped transcripts and random access to frames, with the navigated frames returned into the reasoning models context. Over the full LVBench run its navigation is transcript-first. 1,353 of the 1,549 thought summaries refer to the transcript, ASR or subtitles; the tool-use text tokens, which carry what it retrieves from the transcript, have median of 16.6k per question; and it reads median of 93 frames on questions whose annotated evidence window 27 VideoNexus: Video Perception Beyond the Reasoning Context our transcript places speech in, against 286 on questions whose window has no speech. visual scan is available, and 447 thought summaries describe sparse or low-frame-rate scanning. Transcript-based navigation is frequent, but the traces do not establish why the model selects this strategy. VideoNexuss Overview makes the global scan cheap for the Planner, and the Planner uses it where the transcript cannot help: it fires on 29% of the questions whose evidence window contains speech, on 62% of those whose window does not, and on 81% of the questions about the 12 videos without an audio track (figure 14). sections.title: M The native timeline probe
sections.content: VideoNexuss Findings are only composable if every perception call reports time on the same clock, so we checked what the perception model does when it is given an interval of longer video rather than clip. Across 12 probe responses with neutral prompts no instruction about which origin to use all 12 reported times on the absolute source timeline, including the 6 that were asked to state their reference explicitly. The 6 responses given physically cropped clip instead reported times relative to that clips own start. We therefore pass intervals by timestamp and never hand the model pre-cut file, which removes the offset bookkeeping that clip-based harnesses need.

sections.title: N Limitations
sections.content: Each Inspect adds model request and can increase latency; the available measurements do not establish matched wall-clock comparison with static ingestion. We do not report wall-clock comparison against the baseline: in our own runs only 22 of 160 median seconds per question are recorded API time, the rest being local decode, transcode and upload, and the baselines per-call latency varied by 50% across hosts with load, so neither number isolates the harness. The benchmark has text prior. blind control given the question alone, with no video, audio or transcript, answers 40.5% of full LVBench  (table 1)  . This demonstrates substantial performance without video. The control uses the same high thinking level as the main arms; its accuracy neither bounds all possible text-only strategies nor provides causal decomposition of multimodal performance. The VideoSeek re-run answered 52 of the 1,549 questions without perception call and was correct on 25 (48%). This self-selected subset further illustrates that some answers can be produced without viewing the video. Costs are provider-specific. All dollar figures are list prices of one model; the image-tier confound and its bound are in appendix C. The baseline comparison is asymmetric on speech, in our favour. VideoNexus reads the native audio track and an ASR transcript; the VideoSeek re-run, following its released configuration, reads neither, and its own subtitle path filters windows with disjunction where conjunction is intended, so enabling it would place the entire transcript in 28 VideoNexus: Video Perception Beyond the Reasoning Context every call. We therefore report the no-speech slices separately (appendix E), where our margin is 3.9 points rather than the 8.7 it reaches where speech falls inside the evidence window this variation cannot quantify the modality advantage because the question groups differ and speech elsewhere may still aid localization. 12 of LVBenchs 103 videos, covering 175 questions, carry no audio stream at all, so for those questions the asymmetry does not exist. The ablations are paired but not held out. The ablations of sections 4.4 and 4.6 and appendix are measured on the 200 dev questions used during development. Pairing controls question composition but does not remove development selection or configuration differences. These are not held-out results. We report discordant-pair counts where per-question records are available; the Gemini 3.8 card comparison has aggregate counts only. The resumed baseline run also reveals answer variability: 55 of its 1,549 questions were answered twice at identical settings, and 7 of the 55 came back with different answer, which cautions against overinterpreting small differences but does not estimate the variance of full-run accuracy. Where duplicate exists we count the earliest-finished attempt, rule fixed independently of whether it was correct. Errors made inside perception call persist unless the Planner decides to look again; overconfident absent findings and inconsistent counts across calls are the main residual errors. All components are accessed through commercial APIs whose versions may change. Development decisions were made on 200-question subset of LVBench, which we report separately from full-set results. On short clips and on questions that depend on the global order of events, single static pass remains competitive or better.
